part.title: Restoring damaged coral reefs

turns.text: Good morning, everyone. Last week we looked at how coral reefs form, so today I'd like to turn to something a bit more hopeful: how scientists are trying to repair reefs that have already been damaged. I'll start with why reefs decline, then talk about coral gardening, then some newer methods, and I'll finish with how we actually measure success.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Right. The biggest threat by far is bleaching. Corals have tiny algae living inside their tissue, and most people think of these algae as the thing that gives coral its colour. That's true, but more importantly, they produce the bulk of the coral's food, something like ninety per cent of it. So when the water gets too warm and the coral pushes the algae out, it turns white and basically starts to starve.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: The second threat is the crown-of-thorns starfish. Despite the dramatic name, it's simply a starfish that feeds on coral, and normally there aren't many of them around. But fertiliser washing off farms and down the rivers here in Queensland seems to help their young survive. So every few years we get huge outbreaks, and they can strip a section of reef in a matter of months.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Then there are cyclones. A severe cyclone doesn't just damage individual corals; it can smash the whole structure into loose rubble. And that's a real headache, because rubble rolls around with every wave, so any baby coral that settles on it gets crushed or buried. Some sites can stay bare for decades because of that.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: OK, so what can we do about it? The best-known approach is coral gardening. Divers collect small fragments from healthy corals and grow them in an underwater nursery. The first nurseries were basically flat tables sitting on the seabed, but these days most teams use frames that look rather like trees, with branches made of plastic pipe, and the fragments hang from those branches in the open water.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: How long do they stay in the nursery? Students often guess a few weeks, but it's a good deal longer than that. Fast-growing species might be ready in six months, but on average it's around nine months before the fragments are big enough to go back onto the reef. Then divers attach them to the reef one by one, usually with a kind of underwater cement.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Now, coral gardening is sometimes criticised for being expensive. Actually, the costs have come down a lot in the last ten years. The real weakness is that it's slow. A good team might plant a few thousand corals in a season, but when you remember that the Great Barrier Reef covers an area bigger than Italy, you can see the problem.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: And that brings me to some newer methods. One is sometimes called coral IVF. Many corals reproduce in a mass spawning event, which happens just once a year, usually a few nights after a full moon in late spring. Researchers head out after dark and collect the eggs and sperm floating on the surface.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: They raise the larvae in floating pools for about a week, sorry, five days, and then release them over a damaged patch of reef. The tricky part is that larvae drift away very easily. So the team covers the area with what they call a mesh tent, which keeps the larvae in place for several days while they settle.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Another line of research is breeding tougher corals. A few years ago some labs were looking at corals that could resist pollution, but the main focus now is heat. The idea is to cross corals that came through a bad bleaching year, in the hope that their offspring will cope better with warmer water.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: And here's one I really like. A reef isn't only coral; it needs fish, which graze on the seaweed and keep the coral clear. Healthy reefs are surprisingly noisy, with shrimps crackling and fish grunting. Researchers found that if you put underwater speakers on a damaged reef and play recordings of a healthy one, young fish are drawn to it, and a lot of them stay.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Finally, how do we know if any of this actually works? That's a question people in the field have argued about for years. For a long time, projects simply reported the number of corals they'd planted. It makes a nice headline, but it tells you very little, because many of those corals might be dead a year later. So now we look at survival rates and at how much of the seabed is covered by living coral.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: But for me, the real test comes later. Growing bigger is good, and getting through a hot summer is even better. A restored reef is only truly successful when the corals we've put out there begin to reproduce on their own, because then the reef can start rebuilding itself without our help.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Right, that's all for today. For next week, please read the chapter on reef monitoring, and have a look at the photos from our own nursery off Heron Island, which I've put online.
turns.speaker: lecturer
